rationale: Start with a broad, mid-temperature scouting gradient that should elute all 10 compounds within the time limit while revealing the overall retention window and any critical pairs. The wide phi range and moderate slope maximize information for later trimming and optimization.

All compounds eluted well within the gradient and the estimated elution window is much narrower than 0.05–0.95, so trim the high-organic end to keep peaks inside a more focused gradient and improve selectivity around the closest cluster near rows 5–7. Holding tG and T constant isolates the effect of narrowing the phi window.

The first run already had perfect resolution, so the path to a higher CRF is to cut analysis time. A shorter gradient at the same phi window and temperature tests how much we can compress the chromatogram before any critical pair approaches the resolution limit.

The 10 min gradient is fast but over-compresses the 5–7 cluster, while 20 min gives excess resolution, so test an intermediate slope to recover that critical pair without paying too much time penalty. Keeping phi window and temperature fixed cleanly probes slope sensitivity of the crowded region.

The critical pair improves strongly with shallower slope: R(6,7) rose from 0.46 at 10 min to 1.20 at 14 min, while 20 min over-solves at unnecessary time cost. A 16 min gradient should move that pair closer to full baseline resolution while likely retaining the zero time penalty.

The remaining limitation at 14 min is the 6/7 pair, and since slope helped but 16 min incurred a time penalty, temperature is the next lever to try for a selectivity gain without lengthening the gradient. A 5 °C decrease should modestly spread the chromatogram and may improve that pair enough to reach a higher resolution term while likely keeping the run in the no-penalty region.

Lowering temperature worsened selectivity by collapsing a different pair, so test the opposite direction at the current best gradient. A small increase to 45 C may reorder or open the crowded 5–7 cluster while preserving the short, zero-penalty run.

Temperature changes both hurt the crowded cluster, so 40 C appears best and the optimum is likely near the slope boundary between 10 and 16 min. Testing 12 min maps the other side of the 14 min point and may reveal whether 14 min is truly near-optimal or if a slightly steeper gradient gives a better CRF tradeoff.

The best runs indicate the optimum is mostly a slope/selectivity issue within the central cluster, and the actual elution window only reaches about mid-organic, so reducing phi1 moderately from 0.95 to 0.85 should shallow the effective gradient without increasing tG. This may improve the 6/7 separation while keeping the run short and all peaks within the gradient.

The moderate phi1 reduction to 0.85 improved the critical pair enough to achieve full resolution, but incurred a small time penalty; 0.90 should be a better compromise between selectivity and speed. This directly refines around the current best point while keeping the successful temperature and gradient time fixed.

The current best is very close to ideal, with only the 6/7 pair limiting the resolution term slightly. A small further reduction in gradient steepness at the same phi window should nudge that pair toward full resolution; the modest extra time may still preserve an excellent overall CRF and could reveal whether 0.989 is the local maximum.

At phi1 0.90, 16 min overpaid in time for extra resolution, so the optimum likely lies between 12 and 14 min or very close to 14. Testing 12 min at this improved phi window checks whether a slightly steeper run can retain nearly the same selectivity but gain enough speed to challenge the current best.

Both lowering phi1 and lengthening tG independently improved the critical 6/7 pair, so combining the better phi window with the shorter 12 min gradient may recover enough selectivity to outperform 12/0.90 while staying faster than 14/0.85. This targets the apparent speed-resolution sweet spot around the current best region.

The best region is around phi1 0.85–0.90 and tG 14 min, so now probe the low-organic edge: the first peak still elutes fairly early, suggesting phi0 may be higher than needed. Raising phi0 to 0.10 narrows the gradient window and may shift selectivity within the crowded mid-eluting cluster enough to improve the last remaining suboptimal pair without increasing run time.

The new best came from narrowing the low end of the window, and earlier results showed a modest benefit from lowering phi1 from 0.95 to 0.90, so test the combined narrower window at the same tG and T. This may further improve the 6/7 selectivity while still keeping the run short enough for a near-maximal CRF.

We have already achieved the maximum CRF, so further injections should map robustness near the optimum without repeating the exact method. Raising phi0 one more step keeps the same successful upper bound and slope region while testing whether the optimum sits on a broader plateau or if early-window trimming starts to erode selectivity.

Two adjacent phi0 settings now give the maximum CRF, so continue stepping phi0 upward to define the extent of the optimum plateau and identify where the first peaks become too weakly retained. This is the most informative remaining robustness test while staying near the proven best region.

The plateau peaks at phi0 0.10–0.15 with phi1 0.85, and phi0 0.20 starts to under-retain the earliest peak, so keep phi0 at the robust center and now test a slightly lower phi1. This checks whether the upper edge can be trimmed one more step while preserving full resolution and zero time penalty.

Lowering phi1 to 0.80 preserved full resolution but added a small time penalty at phi0 0.15, so shift back to the other optimum phi0 value to see whether it gives a slightly better speed/selectivity balance at the same upper bound. This explores the remaining unexplored corner adjacent to the two 1.000 methods.

We have mapped the optimum plateau at phi1 0.85 and seen both lower and higher phi1 effects at phi0 0.05–0.10, but not yet at the other optimal phi0. Testing phi1 0.90 with phi0 0.15 completes the local surface around the two 1.000 methods and checks whether this corner also stays at the maximum.

With the maximum already reached at 40 C, use remaining injections to test robustness of the best recipe to temperature. Evaluating the optimum window at 45 C shows whether the method is sensitive to modest heating near the chosen plateau or if the top region remains broad in T as well.

The optimum window is highly temperature-sensitive at 45 C, so test the opposite perturbation to bracket robustness around the 40 C maximum. This completes the local temperature profile of the best method and confirms whether 40 C is a sharp optimum or just the least bad of nearby settings.

With temperature bracketing complete, use the last injections to probe how far run time can be shortened from the optimal plateau before resolution drops below the maximum. Testing the faster 12 min gradient at the second 1.000 composition assesses whether that composition is more tolerant to steeper slope than the phi0 0.10 case.

The optimum is already known, so use the penultimate run to complete the slope bracket around the best phi0 0.10, phi1 0.85 composition. This confirms how quickly the method loses CRF on the shallow side and fully defines robustness around the winning recipe.

Use the final run to complete the shallow-slope bracket at the second maximum-CRF composition. This fully maps the local optimum plateau and its robustness, while staying adjacent to the established best conditions.
